items.question: What If Britain pursued a more hostile stance against the American Colonies following the Boston Tea Party, going on the offensive in 1774?
human_answers: This is why it might have been shortsighted for the British Empire to put so much investment in achieving the total conquest and liquidation of the French Colonial position in the Ohio Country and Canada in the 1754-1763 timeframe, to disproportionate benefit of their Colonial 'Fortunate Sons'. While for Britain, it had the side benefit of defeating French forces, which feels nice, and drawing French fleets out for fights they would lose, and capturing some value from the fur trade, Britain particularly "got over its skis" in providing all this support for the Colonies *without* first compelling the Colonies, then under some fears for their frontier populations, to revise their Charters to accept the principle and practice of taxation by the Westminster Parliament, as a regular, reliable contribution to common defense of the empire, its frontiers, and its trade-based prosperity. Instead, by 1763, Britain brought home French North America like Christmas toys and puppies on its own schilling (though Colonial Assemblies chipped in some from their allowance, but often got reimbursed). But then, late 1763 turned out to be a cold, cold, bitter post-Christmas January hangover, when London Parliament started to tell the Colonies, "now start paying tax for all your presents........oh and by the way, sorry, can't let you play with the new Christmas puppy (settle the new lands in the Ohio, west of the Alleghenies), because it turns out the puppy bites and scratches and we can't afford to keep going to the clinic." ---The Americans certainly were not going to react well to the new message of 'fun's over, time to pay up'. While Britain and the American colonies had certain minimum legal rights, even for tenant farmers (still far less than for small freeholders though) I certainly do not think the three protections you mentioned were observed universally, neither in Britain nor even in all the Colonies, in the 1700s pre and post independence. Making this assertion might be a bit of falling for and repeating English/British self-congratulatory propaganda. Evictions were a fact of life in the English-speaking world in the 1700s and all other centuries. The 1700s were known for the enclosure of common lands [yes, that by itself is not eviction but can lead to starvation-inducing poverty even if one is in a cottage, but it can also lead to failure to meet rent obligations and consequent eviction] and consequent driving of English peasants from the countryside to create an ever increasing town and urban laboring population for industry. White tenants on southern landholdings in the Colonies could be subject to evictions as could tenants in Hudson Valley patroonships. Yes, I'm thinking this is descriptive of the Scandinavian situation until after 1800, or nearly that late, which made it, legally speaking more like serfdom systems East of the Elbe than like tenancy systems in Britain or Western Europe. Serfs lacking really any rights of appeal or any rights at all, whereas tenants in England, parts of France, and I would think the Low Countries and Switzerland would have some rights of appeal, even though their landlords would have superior rights through the 1600s and 1700s.

If the British objective was to set off a full-scale war in every colony right off the bat in which they would lose that is exactly what they should do. The British had no means to do what you're suggesting. The incident that set off the fighting was the British trying to disarm the colonists. In the first year of the war the British lost control in all 13 Colonies. Britian had to spend a year mobilizing an army 1/3 of which were German mercenaries for the invasion of the New York. After winning a number of tactical victories they were unable to bring a single colony back under their control. At no time were they ever able to bring even 10% of the population under occupation. After 1777 all they could hold were coastal enclaves, although there was fratricidal warfare in Georgia & South Carolina. They could hold no territory without the Presence of British or Hessian regulars. Loyalist forces were weak everywhere. The coastal enclaves they held became shells eventually with most of the people leaving, and little trade with the interior. What had brought about the war were British policies to control American trade to force them to trade only with England. That alienated the merchant class. Planters had to sell into a closed market were the buyers set the price, and controlled credit terms. That alienated the planter class. They tried to strangle early industrialization so the colonies could only sell raw materials, and buy English finished goods. That alienated the rising manufacturing class. They blocked westward expansion beyond the Proclamation Line. That alienated the landed class. The overall effect was to squeeze specie out of the colonies creating a growing barter system which alienated everyone. Closing courts, and assemblies, and finally trying to disarm the militia left the colonies with the choice of ether abject surrender or rebellion. It wasn't easy but the British Crown went from being very popular in 1765 to every colony taking up arms against them in 1775.

There are tons of things they could do. They could dissolve the militias and ban the Americans from owning weapons. They could introduce an actual tax to fund a permanent military presence - the Americans paid no land rent, only tarriffs. They could abolished the American right to elect judges and sheriffs, instead appointing crown loyalists by decree. They could have given soldiers immunity from local prosecution and law enforcement, instead tasking their commanding officers (who would of course do pretty much nothing) with upholding the law for their soldiers. They could have created an American trading company owned by the crown and banned Americans from any imports and exports except through this company and cracked down on smuggling. The facts are that the Americans enjoyed the most liberal and democratic system in the world at the time of their revolt. They wanted something even more democratic and liberal. But to most people at the time, especially colonial subjects, they would seem like spoiled toddlers throwing a tantrum. Swedish peasants paid roughly 30-40% of the value of an average harvest in land rent at this time. Icelanders could only trade with the very corrupt royal Danish tradign company, which paid aroudn 5% of the value of their wool and forced the Icelanders to buy moldy flour in return. Austrian and Prussian peasants were banned from owning arms, and their courts were handled by government-appointed bailiffs, unless nobility had the right to neck and hand (to be police, prosecutor, judge and executioner all in one, Judge Dredd style) on their estate.

This is a quote from Wikipedia, as of January 20th, 2026: "With the ascension of peace in 1763 the army was dramatically reduced to a peacetime home establishment of just over 11,000 men, with a further 9,750 for the Irish establishment and 10,000 for the colonies. This meant 20 regiments of infantry totaling just over 11,000 men were stationed in Great Britain, 21 regiments were stationed in Ireland, 18 regiments were stationed in the Americas, and 7 regiments were stationed in Gibraltar. Alongside this, the army could call on 16 regiments of the cavalrymen and 2,712 men in the artillery. This gave a theoretical strength of just over 46,000 men exclusive of the artillery." British Army during the American Revolutionary War - Wikipedia en.wikipedia.org Source as listed in the footnote is here: The British Army at the Start of the Revolution - AmericanRevolution.org Learn about the formation and makeup of the British Army at the start of the American Revolution, with this book chapter from E. Curtis, Ph.D. www.americanrevolution.org "The English establishment comprised 25,871 infantry organized into 46 regiments and 20 independent companies; 4,151 cavalry organized into 16 regiments; and 2,256 artillerymen organized into one regiment of 4 battalions." "The Irish establishment consisted of 13,423 infantry divided into 28 regiments; 2,718 cavalry divided into 12 regiments; and 228 artillerymen embodied into one regiment of four companies. "Such were the numbers of the British army in 1775 and such they had approximately been ever since the close of the Seven Years’ War. "An examination of the location of the British army in 1775 reveals the fact that while small detachments of it were to be found in many distant quarters of the globe, the bulk of it was distributed unequally among three different countries. There were roughly speaking 15,000 men in England, 12,000 in Ireland, and 8,000 in America. The remaining 10,000 were distributed among the West Indies, Africa, Minorca, Gibraltar, and Scotland." Each regiment had a listed strength of 477 men. The British concentrated four of these, or just under 2,000 men, in Boston in 1773 to close the port and essentially establish martial law in Massachusetts. This was achieved by moving them New York City, where these regiments had been stationed. The other 6,000 to 8,000 men to cover Canada, Fort Ticonderoga, the forts around the Great Lakes, Florida, Jamaica, and the West Indies. After abandoning Boston, in 1776 the British increased the size of their army from roughly 45,000 to 60,000 troops, mainly be recruiting in Germany. Out of these, they were able to concentrate about 40,000 to take New York, including troops that had been sent to and which failed to take Charleston. Another 10,000 or so chased the Americans out of Canada. Peak strength of the Briitsh army during the American War of Independence was around 80,000. Note that the British were expecting a rematch with France during this time. In fact, Amherst, the commander of the British army, pointed out that the British simply didn't have the strength to garrison the thirteen colonies and advised against trying to reconquer them. The point is that in 1773, the British had the strength to do a show of force in Boston only. And since 90% of the disturbances were coming from New England, the calculation had to be that this would be sufficient. It was only in New England where the situation was turning violent, and it was only after the formation of the Continental Army, and armed clashes between British and American troops, that they declared all thirteen colonies to be in rebellion and started expanding the army. And they really had to wait for the situation to turn that bad to be able to do that.

People in general don't see stuff like that in objective terms. What people see is that suddenly the government made it more expensive or difficult for them to conduct the usual business of life (which was the effect of all the legislation regarding the colonies from 1763 on) and of course they will complain about it, regardless of how good they have it on a cosmic scale. You might as well tell workers in a first world country that they shouldn't go on strike because slavery is still practiced in certain places. That's a very bad idea, because, you know, there are still hostile natives in the borders . In order to not to lose the territory to them, they'd have to station a permanent army all over the border, and that most likely would end up being more expensive than just let the settlers take care of their own defense. And that's not even going into the possibility of slave rebellions in the places where slavery is still legal...
items.original_question: What if Britain pursued a more hostile stance against the American Colonies following the Boston Tea Party, going on the offensive in 1774? As the title suggests, I've been trying to figure out what an earlier beginning to the American Revolutionary War might entail. As to how this happens specifically, military action was advocated as soon as news of the tea party reached London by some hard-line MPs such as Germain OTL. items.question: What If not Russia, which country could have become the Soviet Union?
human_answers: Also, with or without overseas colonies, Communist France / Germany would be in a relatively poor position to defend themselves, as their territory is relatively small, so they can't trade space for time, or evacuate their industry far behind the frontlines (the way Russia did), and most of their core industrial and agricultural are close to borders or to coasts. They also would also be outnumbered by their combined enemies (eg. Communist France having to fight an anti-communist coalition of Britain, Germany and other countries), while the USSR actually outnumbered the Axis in WWII (and always had more reserves). Communist France would be very vulnerable to an Anglo-German invasion, with the British blockading the country and possibly landing in Brittany, Normandy, Picardy and/or Nord-Pas-de-Calais, and the Germans invading from the east (possibly with Italians and Spaniards also attacking, and those attacks could probably be contained thanks to the Alps and Pyrenees, but would divert men away from the main fronts). Communist Germany would essentially be in the same position as OTL WWI Germany, stuck between the Anglo-French and Russians. Now, a Franco-German communist union already has more potential. In addition, if France and Germany become a communist state together, there's a strong possibility that other nations will join them. Belgium and Netherlands are quite likely give their position, and also Italy, Spain and Portugal, due to their economical conditions and political instability.

Leading up to WW1, moat of the communist parties of the great powers were following the line of the second international, and therefore we're unable to seize power, the exception being of course the Russians. Had lines equivalent to those of Lenin prospered in the communist parties of other great powers, it is likely that any number of them could have had a successful communist revolution during or immediately after WW1. Germany is the most obvious candidate, as they had a big revolution irl even though it failed. Italy is another candidate, and to a lesser extent France. However, any of these countries would have issues with surviving alone under siege socialism as the Russians did. It was assumed at the time that a revolutionary state could only survive with the export of the revolution, lest it be surrounded and defeated by hostile imperialist powers. Stalin proved this wrong, Russia did benefit from it's unique geography in this sense. Could greater German industrial power make a German Soviet Republic defensible? I'd argue yes. Whilst Russian geography helped defensible, it was the economic boom, industrialisation, and enthusiasm of the people that helped it survive imperialist intervention. History ahs shown how enthusiastic armies fighting for a cause can and do defeat foreign powers. France is far more vulnerable to attack than Russia, and yet the French revolutionary wars showed how successful a mobiles french populace could be against the powers of the day. Whilst Germany does not have all the strategic depth and resources of Russia, could Britain France and Russia really afford fulls cake invasions just after WW1? They would run the risk of Revolution spreading among their own tired soldiers. AS for exporting revolution, depending on timing, an established communist Germany could be in a good position to support revolutions in Hungary and Finland , to give a couple of examples.

I think the stickiest element here is the combo of ideology and great/superpower status necessary to mimic the Soviets. If all that was needed was a large and relatively undeveloped country, China or India are easy picks. The problem is ideology. China only went communist in OTL because of the Soviets. No Soviets, no communist China (or India). These places could hypothetically adopt some other far-left socialist ideology, but it probably wouldn't be identifiably Marxist. Meanwhile, if all that was needed was ideology, many other European countries could conceivably fulfill the role. But if, say, France and France alone went communist, they would be considered threatening, but their industry was already decently developed and central planning isn't exactly good at innovating. Their threat level would not be able to rise much compared to the Soviets who had the wiggle room of being able to look at more developed countries and copy their homework. The Soviets also had a massive pool of labor and natural resources that France would lack. A France that probably lost its colonies and has a lagging industry is a middling concern, ultimately. Ditto with Germany. What's really needed, IMO, for another communist entity to arise to pose a similar threat to the Soviets is a multinational revolution in places where Marxism had decent traction. This means multiple Western European countries experiencing revolution and then deciding to cooperate heavily. Alternatively, a multinational coalition of revolutionary socialist states in South America (which must include Brazil since it has the largest population) could potentially adopt a similar role to the Soviets, although they'd be working with both a somewhat smaller population than the Soviets and a less developed industry than Western Europe. As an outside bet, maybe a revolutionary Spain somehow inspires its former colonies to follow suit and they join hands? Wouldn't need Brazil if you could pick up most of Hispanic America.

I do agree to some extent. Germany and France, though geopolitically disadvantaged, both demonstrated explosive potential for modernization. France, during the Napoleonic Wars, nearly conquered Europe by maximizing the advantages of advanced military doctrines, exceptional leadership, and the power of the nation-state. It’s interesting to think, though, how things might have unfolded if Napoleon had pursued democratic ideals rather than imperial ambitions. What if, instead of installing his relatives as kings, he had focused on exporting republicanism to other nations? Germany also revived after its defeat in World War I, almost conquering Europe by defeating France in just six weeks. However, their ideology, which was not universal but rather intended for domestic consumption, was deeply flawed in terms of fairness and equality. However, there is an issue with the immediate post-World War I period. It was the time when Germany's political system was most vulnerable, yet it was also the period when Germany faced the greatest risk of invasion. If the Kiel mutiny had led to a communist regime in Germany, the Entente Powers would likely have continued the war, eventually attempting to capture Berlin. Indeed, the Soviet Union only became one of the dominant global powers after World War II. Before that, it primarily focused on spreading communism in its neighboring countries.

I think Tsarist Russia was the only country able to become a truly 'marxist' superpower. And even they immediately morphed into a 'Marxist-Leninist' and eventually 'Stalinist' one-party state. If for some reason the Russian Revolution never happened, failed, or never became 'Marxist', Marxism as we know it would remain a political philosophy rather than an ideology, although it would be embraced by various socialist or workers-right parties in the various European parliamentary systems. The closest to a 'soviet-style' communist state I can think of would be Mao's China in the 1940's/1950's where due to it effectively still being run by the last remaining pre-WWII era warlord, China would still be. One-party state with the one party adhering to Chinese-style communism. Before that, any country where the Socialist/communist parties gain a majority in the democratic parliament would be the 'communist' world leader, be it Labour Britain, France, Weimar Germany or even a USA with a pro-labour pro-social(ist) president.
items.original_question: If not Russia, which country could have become the Soviet Union? In OTL, the Soviet Union was essentially the leader of communism, the state that embodied and exported the ideology. In France, after the birth of the “first republic in Europe,” the country faced massive wars against the old Western monarchies. As a result, although Napoleon, an extraordinary hero, almost succeeded in conquering Europe, France ultimately fell. Soviet Russia also faced a similar crisis. After the October Revolution, the first communist state was born, and the great powers, much like the monarchies a century before, sought to destroy Soviet Russia. However, unlike France, Soviet Russia survived the Russian Civil War. Afterward, the Soviet Union was no longer simply "Communist State A." They developed the potential of the land that was Russia. They transformed the underdeveloped economy of the Russian Empire into one of growth. Using that newfound capability, they exported revolution to various countries around the world. From Eastern Europe to Asia, the surrounding countries of Russia were all affected by communism. Furthermore, after 1945, they became a superpower alongside the United States, exporting revolution globally. Let’s consider a historical counterfactual. After Alexander II, the imperial succession changed. Unlike in OTL, Tsarevich Nicholas survived, and instead of the reactionary Alexander III, he ascended the throne. This alternate Nicholas II continued the reforms initiated by Alexander II, complementing, improving, and strengthening them. Unlike in OTL, Russia underwent a different trajectory. The Russian Empire was preserved, and Soviet Russia never came into being. In this scenario, which country could have replaced the Soviet Union? Which nation would need to become communist in order to "survive against surrounding capitalist powers" and "become a great power capable of exporting revolution?" Sometimes, in alternate history works (especially in game mods by Paradox Interactive), there are many timelines where a socialist revolution occurs in a country other than Russia. However, in my view, it’s questionable how many countries could do what the Soviet Union did. France? Germany? They have many geopolitical enemies. Even if they were to become communist after World War I, could they, like the Soviet Union, export revolution worldwide and become a superpower? It seems more likely that they would struggle just to survive. Britain, the United States? In OTL, Marx argued that a sufficiently developed capitalist system was necessary for a communist revolution to occur, with Britain being his example. Britain was also the world’s leading superpower at the time. However, a communist revolution did not occur in Britain. Because capitalism was so advanced, ironically, the entrenched privileges of the system were also too strong. British socialists who advocated for a revolutionary overthrow of the system did not have the power to challenge the entrenched elites, while others accepted the system and sought reforms within it. Ultimately, the conditions I believe are necessary for a "Soviet candidate" are as follows: 1. Geopolitically, it must be easy to defend. The country should be able to secure its borders and have a strategic position that allows for long-term survival and expansion. 2. It must have the potential to become a great power. The country needs the necessary resources, population, and industrial capacity to rise as a major global player. 3. Capitalism cannot be overly developed, and the elites must be driven toward 'system overthrow' rather than 'system compliance.' There must be enough dissatisfaction with the existing system to foster a desire for revolution, not merely reforms within the system. These are the core elements for a country to replicate the role of the Soviet Union. Where, besides Russia, could there be a land or country that fits these conditions? As a side note, it doesn’t necessarily have to be pure communism in this alternative Soviet ideology. It could be something like Maoism, syndicalism, or a unique form of socialism tailored to the needs of that country.

items.question: What If the Alans had formed a lasting kingdom in Europe?
human_answers: Yeah, Medieval Europe in a lot of ways was already influenced by steppe culture like the Huns, Magyars, Avars. This is most obvious in the way these cultures introduced the stirrup and revolutionized cavalry warfare in the political and social structure. IMO knighthood would probably not have developed in its recognizable form without these cultures. I guess what I was thinking is that with the Alans, it wouldn’t just be inherited bits and pieces . A stable Alan kingdom could’ve institutionalized that heritage in law, military organization, and diplomacy in ways that a post-Hunnic and Avar kingdom probably wouldn’t. And yeah, I didn’t mean “Zoroastrian” in the sense of fire temples and Avesta orthodoxy. More like echoes of older Iranian cosmology or ritual that might’ve persisted under the surface alongside Christianity, at least in the early centuries. Basically, I think the difference is between having remnants of a steppe culture floating around versus having it as the living core of a political state right in the middle of medieval Western Europe. That alone could’ve made for a noticeably different flavor in the region’s history.

Looking at the map I wonder if we would see the Alans have their focus in what is Portugal especially when the Muslims go a-conquering. Also I wonder with this arrangement would we see a Alanic-Latinite language develop since it does seem that the elite would speak Alanic while the lower classes would speak some flavour of vulgar latin. A scenario where high register words that the ancestral Alans cared about, like rulership (leader, group meeting, horse, that kinda stuff) and normal stuff stays roughly Hispanic. It probably would have a reduced grammar too and be completely different from what we see in English, so that's fun to see. All the talk about knighthood also is highly ironic because it ultimately evolved into one of the best ways to defend against steppe raiders, and the diffuse way that every noble defended their lands via castle did stop steppe invasions alongside other factors.
items.original_question: What if the Alans had formed a lasting kingdom in Europe? Most people normally associate the Völkerwanderungen period with the mass migration of Germanic tribes into the Roman frontiers. But a large number of non-Germanic people also joined these groups. One of them were the Alans an Iranian people who crossed the Rhine in the winter of 406 along with the Vandals, Suebi, Goths Burgundians etc. and fanned out into Roman Gaul . They would eventually form a kingdom in North Africa alongside the Vandals. But what if Instead of getting absorbed by the Vandals and the Franks, and disappearing into history, they had actually carved out a stable kingdom, say in southwestern Gaul ? What would that look like? An equestrian -based kingdom with a mix of Iranian steppe traditions and local Roman and Germanic culture. Their language and customs might’ve stuck around longer, even mixing with early medieval Christianity or holding onto some older beliefs. I think that this Alan kingdom could’ve complicated Frankish expansion, maybe even keeping Charlemagne from totally dominating Western Europe or at least delaying it? Their military skills might have decided the outcome in battles and diplomacy, and their cultural blend could’ve made medieval Europe way more diverse , for example maybe in unique artistic terms, linguistic influence and traditions. They don't necessarily have to dominate Europe, but form a lasting kingdom long enough for their language, culture, military tradition, religion to make an impact. The whole medieval map could’ve looked very different, and who knows, maybe Zoroastrian-inspired beliefs and horse culture would still echo in some French villages today.

items.original_question: What if Partition of the Austrian Netherlands in the 18th Century? Hi, everyone. This is my second post sharing some lesser-known yet fascinating PoDs in European history. I stumbled upon a historical academic journal written by Frederik Dhondt, a history professor from the Ghent University in Belgium titled " So Great a Revolution’: Charles Townshend and the Partition of the Austrian Netherlands, September 1725 " (2012, Journal of Low Countries Studies). According to the article, Charles Townshend, the British Northern Secretary (equivalent to the Foreign Minister) and his predecessor James Stanhope (†. 1721) had proposed a partition of the Austrian Netherlands. The plan would see Austria surrendering its holdings in the Low Countries. The article summarised three possibilities. Some background before moving on. In the Nine Years' Year and the War of the Spanish Succession, Austria had allied with the Dutch Republic and Great Britain (or England-Scotland before 1707) to counter French ambitions in the Low Countries and the Rhineland. Towards the end of the Spanish Succession War, Britain became weary of increasing Austrian power. In 1716, it allied with France. The Austro-Spanish alliance confirmed by the Treaty of Vienna rang alarm bells in London. Not only did it reconcile the enmity between Emperor Charles XI and King Philip V, the combined power of Spain and Austria threatened the established balance of power. There were even talks to marry Maria Theresa to Don Carlos (future Charles III). Prime Minister Walpole and Townshend, therefore, desired to weaken the power of Austria. These plans were never made public, Townshend only discussed them with the ambassador in Paris, Horace Walpole. On page 56, Townshend suggested the partition plan could be implemented if the marriage between Maria Theresa and Don Carlos took place. James Stanhope first suggested that the Duke of Lorraine could receive Austria Netherlands. Alternatively, Stanhope suggested awarding it either to the Elector of Cologne or the Elector of Trier. The Electorate would be secularised. Townshend outright dismissed these ridiculous ideas, and offered his own solution. The Dutch will annex some territories including Antwerp. Ypres, Bruges, and Ostend would fall under joint Dutch-British control while the inland and southern portions of the Austrian Netherlands will go to France. What will be the geopolitical and diplomatic consequences of one of these plans was realised? Although I personally doubt the likelihood of this happening, nevertheless the ramifications will be interesting. You can access the article here through your university: https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1179/0309656411Z.0000000002 .

items.question: My Alternative History Scenario: What If Napoleon couldn't make it to France at 1799?
human_answers: It's very obscure and I couldn't track down the reference this morning, which I think came from some book on the First Serbian Uprising. The Turkish fortress on the island blocked easy communication between the Serbs and the Russian forces in Wallachia. items.original_question: My Alternative History Scenario: What if Napoleon couldn't make it to France at 1799? EPISODE THREE​ German Pact ​ ​ A sudden storm breaking out across Europe had created a massive shockwave. Austria, still struggling to recover from the economic and military wounds of the War of the Second Coalition, was deeply displeased by France’s abrupt rekindling of hostilities. Emperor Francis II had been expecting a long period of peace, one he intended to devote to revitalizing Germany. Unfortunately, history had once again disappointed him. His federalist ambitions had not yet completely faded, but this meant confronting French republicanism earlier than anticipated. Moreover, following the referendum held on 18 February 1803 and the subsequent election, the country transitioned into what was called a presidential system. As a result, Fourier—who came to power and was a prominent representative of socialist thought—began spreading his ideas more widely across Europe. This signified a gradual shift of the German peoples toward republicanism. Although the Kingdom of Prussia and the Habsburg Monarchy did not hold each other in high regard, they shared a common enemy: France and republicanism. Approximately one week had passed since the outbreak of the Franco-Spanish War. French armies advanced rapidly, exploiting the dire condition of the Spanish forces to seize Catalonia and push toward Eastern Aragon. The Basque region had also fallen. Emperor Francis convened his cabinet, and they debated at length what course of action should be taken. Johann Amadeus Franz, the Minister of Finance of the era, was firmly opposed to breaking the peace with France, as any potential war would further devastate Austria’s already fragile economy. József Alvinczi, the Chief of the General Staff, argued that this war represented an opportunity to eliminate both France and the spread of republican ideas on the European continent. He maintained that, as demonstrated in the previous conflict, the Austrian army was not in as poor a condition as believed and demanded that an open ultimatum be issued to France. However, the Emperor had a different plan in mind. Although there was no certainty it would succeed, he deemed it worth attempting. For this reason, he decided to send a delegate to the Kingdom of Prussia, carrying a note requesting a private meeting with the King. The delegation set out on 15 March 1803. Meanwhile, across Europe, no clear decision had yet emerged from the British Isles. Prime Minister Henry Addington had no desire to see Spain under French control, but he also believed that the British Army was not yet prepared. After lengthy discussions with other statesmen, he sent an envoy to the Kingdom of Portugal to further expand the Anglo-Portuguese Alliance and present several proposals. In the meantime, the delegation sent by Austria to Prussia returned two weeks later. The Emperor’s proposal to the King of Prussia was to intervene in the Franco-Spanish War by forming a German coalition. The Prussian King, eager to enhance his prestige among the German states, responded favorably and announced his acceptance. Thus, the German Pact was formed. Both sides began final preparations for their already mobilized armies, and within approximately two weeks, everything was ready. A note bearing the personal signatures of both the Emperor and the King was delivered to the French delegates by a joint Austro-Prussian mission. The note demanded that France sever its alliance with the United States, withdraw from Spain, and agree to certain trade arrangements. French President Charles Fourier tore the original document to pieces in parliament. This act provided the Habsburg Monarchy and the Kingdom of Prussia with sufficient legitimacy to launch a military intervention against France. Emperor Francis II was deeply uneasy about Russia’s ambiguous stance. He neither wanted Russia to emerge excessively strong nor excessively weak. Poland could be the first step, and the Russian flag might one day fly over Hungary or the borders of the Holy Roman Empire. Taking such a risk seemed irrational. Therefore, depending on the course of the war, he considered enticing Russia into joining their side by offering the Balkan territories of the already weakened Ottoman Empire—despite his preference for preserving the balance of power in the Balkans and Eastern Europe. The French threat, however, took precedence. Although the United States did not yet pose a direct threat to Europe, it continued to threaten the colonial powers in the Americas. While it had not yet entered the conflict, such an involvement was not impossible. On the other hand, the Emperor foresaw that the French government’s aggressive and overly idealistic actions would ultimately lead to its downfall. By initiating this war, France had effectively shot itself in the foot, and these events would pave the way for a rise in anti-French sentiment throughout Europe.

items.question: What If the Greek 'Great Plan' had succeeded and the Greek War of Independence had triggered an early collapse of the Ottoman Empire?
human_answers: A more decisive Ottoman defeat against Greece can give birth to the "Megali Idea" before 1844. In such a scenario, a larger independent Greek state can invited Louis-Philippe d’Orléans to become its king, before 1830 of course. This arrangement can be supported by both France and its Bourbon king, who might want to sideline a troublesome cousin, and by the United Kingdom. For the British, the presence of a Great European power south of the Straits, one aligned with neither Austria nor Russia can further divide the continental great powers and serve British strategic interests. With France satisfied in Greece and Austria compensated with territories along the Adriatic coast, Britain can focus on securing Egypt for itself. Even if the Suez Canal is not even a dream, control of Egypt is already strategically valuable for strengthening connections with India. By 1829, railway projects are already under consideration, making overland transit increasingly plausible and reinforcing Egypt’s geopolitical importance. And if its happen after 1830, Louis-Philippe has enough sons (6 minus one who died in 1828) to send one to Greece.

Considering their interest is not even religious (GB: Protestant, France: Catholic, Russia: Orthodox) and that really none of these Great Powers saw the Greek War of Independence with positive eyes (to them it was no different than the revolutions in Spain, Portugal and Naples; which, btw, they sent huge armies to crush). There was later a British change, but even the Metternich, Alexander and so on weren't super happy about it. Remember: at this point, the memory of Napoleon is far fresher than that of the Ottoman invasions into the Balkans, so the concern, far above Islam, is revolutionary sentiment. What I do see happening is them deliberating and taking too long to make a decision that the situation ends up devolving on its own (it took them like 3 years to agree to send an invasion to Spain). Then again, the French were sympathetic to Muhammad Ali while the British aided Ali Pasha plenty of times (through Maitland, specifically). They will always prefer a rotting corpse of the Ottoman empire maintaining power over the ambitious and reformist Albanian Pashas in power, this is why they went out of their way to put them out IRL, but when shit hits the fan, they have to re-examine their approach of course.

Agreed that the Great Powers, including even Russia under Alexander, don't want a full Ottoman collapse. That's not the same as saying they would intervene to stop it. It's hard to conceive of a situation in which Great Britain, France, or Russia would go to war to suppress Christian rebels fighting against the Sultan, particularly after the various atrocities committed at Chios and other places. There were also similar atrocities committed by the Greeks against Muslims, but this did not register in the European consciousness of the time and would not be a factor. It's also not a given that any intervention would be successful at stopping chaos and preserving the Empire, even if it did somehow occur. This would be a formidable job if the situation became so extreme that the Ottomans asked for such support. More likely the intervention would be directed towards managing the collapse and achieving a partition either formally or in terms of spheres of influence.

items.question: What If the French become one of the largest communities in the US
human_answers: Hordes of Catholics, even if not all that devout, descending on the US will cause some tension. On the flip side, though, France is one of the civilized nations, and they're seen as more desirable shade of white. Timing matters, too. Napoleonic era, when immigration is still low, is a whole lot different than the final decades of the 19th century, when millions is a drop in the bucket. Location matters, too. Are the French hordes joining into the crowded East, where they likely assimilate? Or are they carving out a big chunk of the midwest/west as largely French? Reason for the diaspora might matter. If we mess with the Napoleonic era, especially if we butterfly it (not killing off a generation or two of males would be a good start in having excess population to export), the state of the world could affect the state of the USA (maybe even the size if no Mex-Am War/Texas). With such a generic What if, we can only talk in generics. If we stipulate a recognizable world, more or less the same, except a massive French diaspora for some reason that hasn't caused OTL to derail.... I would guess the French would be like any other large group. There'll be tension, but everyone will adapt. It's an age of racism, and French are in the top class, so I suspect they'll have an easier time of it. (caveat edit: In no way am I saying French are better than any other nation, but reality is that skin color mattered. My understanding is that not all whites were considered equal)

I would assume rather than staying in the east, the French would largely settle in former Louisiana- centring probably on New Orleans. Texas and Florida as well are likely spots for French settlement. Of the 13 colonies, I would guess it’s the southern ones which would be most amenable to French settlement- though how that affects racial dynamics in the south, and how that affects potential north south tensions is difficult to say. It’s difficult as well to say what the economic impact of French settlement would be- I’d say as a community they’d probably be more educated and thus better off than the Irish or Italians, perhaps more comparable to German or Swedish immigrants. Perhaps the planter class ends up going fully bilingual. Depending on how the 19th century goes you could end up with an Alt-confederacy that stays independent because it has so many French speakers and Catholics that the north simply isn’t interested in reintegrating them.
items.original_question: What if the French become one of the largest communities in the US Let’s suppose that millions of French flocked to the US in the 19th century for one reason or another—for example, because harsher Napoleonic Wars and a more severe Congress of Vienna plunged France into a deep economic crisis, while the Irish and Italians would be less numerous in the US, for example because the Irish Great Famine never happened and the Italian peninsula unified and modernized earlier. No PoD before 1780. How would the French be treated in the US? Would they face xenophobia and form a distinct community like the Irish and Italians, or would they be assimilated among the WASPs within one or two generations like the Germans did IOTL? French culture was admired, but I’m not sure that the arrival of millions of French people (with a Latin culture and Catholic religion) would be particularly well received.

She was a widow after only five months of marriage. She knew that she was not pregnant, as her marriage was unconsummated. One month after she was made a widow, Catalina was moved to Durham House in London and was visited by King Henry VII and his wife, Queen Elizabeth of York. Catalina told them that she had bled already and there was no hope for an heir from their late son, so his younger brother, Prince Henry, Duke of York, was officially declared as the heir. When the news to Catalina's parents, King Fernando II of Aragon and Queen Isabella I of Castile, they were disappointed that the alliance seemed to have fallen through and that their daughter was widowed at only sixteen years old. This began a struggle over Catalina. Queen Isabella was adamant that her youngest child be returned to her, since there was not a hope of an English grandchild to seal the alliance with Spain and England. King Henry VII, however, did not want to lose her or her dowry. He offered to marry her to his younger son and she could still be Queen of England one day. Queen Isabella made up her mind and told her husband that she wanted their daughter to be returned home. King Ferdinand sent an ambassador to tell King Henry that the Princess would be returned to Spain, either with her entourage or by force. When King Henry VII heard this, he was furious, but also terrified. He needed this alliance with Spain and he did not want to let his daughter-in-law go. Finally, an agreement was finally reached. The Infanta would return to her parents and half her dowry would be returned with her and she would retain her status of Dowager Princess of Wales and would still receive her marriage jointure for the remainder of her life. Her English attendants, like Margaret Pole, would remain in England. When she was told Princess Catalina had a mix of grief and relief. She was happy to return home to her parents, especially since her older sister, Juana, who was now Princess of Asturias, was back home as well. On August 1, 1502, Princess Catalina and her entourage arrived at Dover, preparing to board the ship that will cross the sea once again. Prince Henry, the young Prince of Wales accompanied her, just like he escorted her down the aisle to marry his late older brother. The eleven year old, who was talkative and social, was unusually quiet through the journey. Princess Catalina gave him a little kiss on his forehead and told him that she will never forget him or her time in England and she knew that one day, he will be the greatest King that England ever had, before she boarded the ship. Thankfully, this journey was much easier than her original one taking her to England. She and her entourage arrived in Laredo on the 15th of August. Princess Catalina found herself smiling, as she saw the familiar Castilian villages and knew she was home. However, she then was wondering what would happen to her and her future. Due to the deaths of her older brother, sister and nephew, she knew that taking holy vows was not an option, as he parents only had three surviving daughters. Would she just remain a spinster? Would she be married off again to a foreign Kingdom, even France? Her father was definitely ambitious and was a shrewd ruler, so she knew that she would not remain unmarried for long, but she was still looking forward to just feeling her mother's embrace once more.

items.original_question: What if Dynamite Invented During the Renaissance? Dynamite in our world was invented in 1867 by Alfred Noble as a way to stabilize nitroglycerin, an explosive mix of nitric and sulfuric acids with glycerol (the main ingredient in fat-based soap), by mixing it with clay and chalk. Nitroglycerin, however was only discovered 20 years before Noble’s invention earned him the Noble Prize. But what if things were different? Aqua fortis (nitric acid) and oil of vitriol (sulfuric acid) both existed in medieval Europe and were used by OTL alchemists to dissolve gold for their experiments. Maybe an alchemist tries perfecting the ingredient to turn lead into gold but spills his formula all over his workbench. And when he tries to clean up it up with a soapy rag, he blows himself up, leaving his apprentice to record this newfound discovery. In any case, the year is 1450 and King Henry VI’s “alchemy craze” has taken England by storm. In this craze, nitroglycerin is discovered. Maybe it takes several more decades, if not a century, before alchemists learn how to turn this strange concoction into dynamite. What next?

items.original_question: What if No Seven Bishops' Death in 1558? Everyone knows about the death of Cardinal Pole, Archbishop of Canterbury shortly after Queen Mary in 1558. But less known- as in, not even listed when you google them- is that there were six other bishops who died around the same time (including Maurice Griffith, Bishop of Rochester). This led to the opening of several vacancies in the English Catholic Church at the start of Elizabeth I's reign. To the seven bishops who died, can be added Bishop Oglethorpe of Carlisle (who, while he crowned Elizabeth, was no fan of hers after she stormed out of his celebration of Christmas Mass in 1558 because he defied her) and Nicolas Heath, the archbishop of York, who, as the highest ranked cleric in England should've crowned Elizabeth, but declined the "honour". He lost his see in 1559. What would've happened to the Elizabethan Settlement if those seven (or nine) sees had not fallen vacant at exactly the same time (many remaining vacant until 1561). How much opposition would there be to Elizabeth TTL? And how would Elizabeth have dealt with the situation TTL? @BlueFlowwer @isabella @RedKing @HortenseMancini

items.question: The Heir to Sulla: What If Sulla Fought Mithridates VI And Marius Marched On Rome Instead?
human_answers: Alright, so here are some changes: I wash my hands of the issue with the Marian reforms. Let's move on from that. Marius helps coordinate the Dimidiatio Senatus by spreading rumors and disrupting trade and grain shipments. After the creation of the Roman Tribunal Republic, he stays in Italia, raises an army of soldiers, professionally trains them, and leads the early Tribunal Republic. Sulla comes to Rome, and while the battle is intense, Marius and Rome win a pyrrhic victory, with Marius dying later that year. During the Battle of Rome, which even enters the city itself and causes immense destruction, young Gaius Julius Caesar dies. The Tribunal Republic fights remnants of people sympathetic to Sulla, and just continues on as normal. The proscriptions never happen. The closest equivalent is that many wealthy families were killed by poorer people and their wealth confiscated during the Sullarian War. But there's not really a reign of terror, just a violent popular revolt. The way the Roman Tribunal Republic gets set up still gradually happens, and the Tribunal Senate eventually creates a regular militia force within Rome itself, so that way no general can march on Rome like Sulla did. Christianity already exists, but doesn't spread far, remaining a religion in Levant and Egypt. It's never institutionalized. Because of this, and other butterfly effects with regular peoples, Mohammed is never born, so Islam never comes to be. The Tribunal Republic is still militarized, but focuses on strategically allying Celtic and Germanic kings against their allies, trading with them using Rome's vast reach and access to trade routes, and slowly integrating them. Rome stays mostly to the coastline to enforce this and use the sea as easy travel, so the navy becomes larger. Once trade settlements eventually reach southern Morocco and find the sub-Saharan trade route and its goods, the effects from trade deals are amplified. Attila still happens, and while it shakes up Rome, they fight them off thanks to alliances and mercenaries. Cassius still exists, and he helps kickstart Roman mercantile economics after the Hunnic Invasion, beginning the gradual plutocratic trend in Roman politics with merchants. Also, slavery still exists. With wars not bringing in as many war-slaves, laws increasingly punished severe crimes with debt slavery, and also enslaved the children of slaves if both parents were enslaved at the time of birth. Chattel slavery and debt/penal slavery still firmly exists, and slaves are traded across the Mediterranean. Sources of war slaves are largely from rivals of allied Celtic, Germanic, African, or Arabic tribes, plus some hostile invading tribes, such as the Norse, the Avars, the Khazars, and various Turkic tribes, keeping Anatolia as "Anatolia" and Greek/Roman/Persian. By 1000, Rome has slowly expanded militarily, commercially, and culturally. There are Roman trade ports along the coast of the whole Mediterranean, the Red Sea, and Western Europe, including Britannia and Hibernia. There are military presences, but the trade of goods from far away was used as a carrot to keep Celts, Germans, Africans, and Arabs in line (alongside the stick of Roman military garrisons). It's less depopulation and colonialism and more commerce and trading settlement (think Islamic merchants). Zoroastrian Persia, having not collapsed from Islam in this timeline, is still around. However, the House of Karen took over after a civil war in the late 800s, so now they're the Karenian Empire, not the Sasanian Empire anymore. Instead of an emergency military command being called "Caesar," it's instead called a "Consul." However, Consuls explicitly only lead armies, while the Tribunal Senate and the Orator did their thing, with the highly-professional, well-paid Roman city garrison (named the "Custodes Romae") preventing any Consuls or generals from marching on Rome, as well as acting as the final line of defense against barbarian Invasions. The title of "Res Publica Inter Marium" (RPIT) is put on legion banners, and is otherwise just a term that proud Romans use to praise the Roman Tribunal Republic, or the "Res Publica Tribunorum Romanorum" (RPTR). Roman poets and generals say things like "Ave res publica inter marium!" Did I miss anything?

To a certain point, it may have been possible, given what happened in parts of Medieval Europe, but that was only possible because of Christianity, and even then, forced labour continued being an important part of the economy, but in the form of serfdom instead of chattel slavery. Also, some other things I'd like to point out: I can guess the inspiration for this, but in all likelihood it wouldn't work like that - remember that given the way Roman politics works all of those people have their own clients to call on, and who would likely be around the forum in Senate meetings - visa how quickly Scipio Nasica gathered enough support to take on the supporters of Tiberius Gracchus in 133. The senators wouldn't be sitting ducks, and what you'd probably see is a street battle between each side's mobs of supporters, more like the riots of 52 BC or 100 BC than anything else. Also, remember that the Senate wasn't continuously in session - each session had to be convened by a magistrate and each session only lasted one day, for religious reasons. May I remind you that (assuming this happens in 88 BC) Caesar is 12 years old around that time? Even Pompey was twice that age when he first gained military proeminence, and he only did so by raising and equipping a legion out of his own pocket, because he was too young to be officially appointed to any command.

Okay, let me try to tackle this. Keep in mind this is just my opinion, with the primary goal always being plausibility: As mentioned by others, Marian reforms is a historiographic myth. You'll have to find a reason for the optimates to support land reform. If your main PoD is Marius failing to outmaneuver Sulla, then that's a good starting point. A sunken grain ship won't be enough to inspire the people to want to topple the government. A year or two of very little grain coming in could do that. Remember Marius is very old and probably mentally sick by now. I doubt he lives far beyond early 87 BC. Other populares can take up that mantle, but again, they have to deal with all the rest of the First Class in the years following. Remember also in OTL how the Sullans won literally every single military engagement. In another thread I called it a curbstomp, and it really was a curbstomp. There is extreme support for the optimates in this time period in the Senate, and among soldiers too. There would be no reason to go to Anatolia to fight Sulla, since the populares control Rome. They would force Sulla to come to them as in OTL. Citizen militia can't do anything against legions. Rome has no garrison. Caesar is a teenage kid who's never led armies, he would never be given command. Unless you mean Caesar's father, who is kind of a nonentity. There are dozens of grown men who would command before he's even considered. No such thing as patrician armies. You might mean optimas/optimate armies. The vast majority of forces and leaders on both sides are plebeians. Patrician versus plebeian is by this time almost entirely a religious and social distinction, not a political one. I'll end it here, since the rest of it rests on ever deepening misunderstandings. It's not bad for a story that doesn't mind plausibility and wants to go by "Rule of Cool", so if you want to do it, go ahead. The way I'd try to do something similar, realistically: 1. Marius never breaks with Saturninus and Glaucia 2. Saturninus passes increasingly radical laws, with Marius supporting him due to thinking he can control him 3. The Senate comes into open conflict with Saturninus, passing a Senatus Consultum Ultimum against him and Glaucia 4. With the support of Marius's wealth and veterans, Saturninus and Glaucia are able to subdue the Senate; some senators are killed, others exiled 5. The Republic retains her name, or perhaps is renamed Populus Senatusque Romanus, thus putting the people first; tribunician powers are greatly expanded, to the point where consuls have little legislative power 6. Marius and allies legislate for Italian citizenship to increase their support 7. The crowd begins to realize Marius and allies can't provide the easier life and reforms they promised 8. Decreased provincial incomes due to recalcitrant governors and uncertain political situations create an economic slump Then there are several ways this could go, depending on what the author wants. Romans resistant to Italian citizenship start a much smaller Social War; hard economic times cause worse slave rebellions; a few governors gang up to march on Rome and topple this regime? There are multiple interesting paths. Things that would not happen: 1. Romans peacefully integrating barbarians into Roman government. Most you can expect is Friends and Allies, or barbarians living free but under Roman law in Roman provinces. Rome succeeded for a reason, and part of that reason was being chauvinistic. It's not a moral judgment, just something that made them very good at obtaining and maintaining control completely loyal to decisions emanating from the city of Rome. Famously Cato the Censor, a man from Tusculum (not even 15 miles from Rome), whose ancestors were all Roman and whose father and grandfather had had several horses killed under them in combat, was considered as being a barely Roman peasant by the senators of Rome. Even in OTL the first non-Julio-Claudian emperors were of old senatorial families. Then men whose ancestors had been Roman for generations 2. Anything touching the institution of slavery. Unfree labor is, to this very day, the basis of civilization. Not even in their wildest crack-smoking, mushroom-eating, smoke-puffing dreams would anybody in antiquity think of seriously ending unfree labor 3. A divorce of military from politics. That's an extremely modern concept, and even today not true of the vast majority of states. Prior to the 18th century it would be almost laughable to think the two aren't intertwined. Whoever has the force of arms makes the decisions; where there are more groups with force, they bargain to make decisions, or go to war. That's politics. It's also why barbarian emperors happened, because that's who started having military power. While ever Romans held military power, they made the decisions, they were the emperors. When they left that to barbarians, the situation quickly turned in the barbarians' favor 4. A centuries-long run of kumbaya where wars decrease in intensity and rivalries are mostly commercial. Commercial wars turn into military wars really quickly when one side can't establish complete dominance very quickly. Starting out commercial, the money comes in handy paying mercenaries to fight. Things only escalate from there. Commerce, the control of cash and goods and people, is actually one of the only reasons wars were fought historically. The only bigger one I can think of is agriculture (land) itself, that produces those goods and people Anyway, interesting idea. I would say read some more history, and understand how these processes actually evolve and shape the world. Also how the government in Rome worked. History works in grand, broad strokes and movements, so don't expect cultures and governments to turn on a dime. Even the transformation of Rome from a Republic to the Principate was gradual. People forget the civil wars actually took over five decades to get through. It was very much a process, and in the end rested very much on preserving some image and veneer of the old. For example Augustus holding imperium maius everywhere, becoming eventually pontifex maximus, retaining tribunician powers (despite being patrician by adoption), etc. were all very old, traditional things just twisted acceptably by time and political necessity (and with the force of legions backing it, of course). Changing how Rome works? Fine! Changing how Rome is called? Hmmmm, not so good! It took over three centuries, from Augustus to Diocletian, before it became acceptable to verbally acknowledge the emperor as Dominus (Master), and to prostrate before him. That's how long it took from Rome's government to transform from an Italian city-state to a Hellenistic autocracy. Anyway I've written too long anyway. Learn more and never stop thinking, you'll do fine with any timeline you write
items.original_question: The Heir to Sulla: What If Sulla Fought Mithridates VI And Marius Marched On Rome Instead? This is a scenario I've imagined for a Rome that never becomes an empire. And also because I wanted to create a Roman Republic I could call "Intermarium" because I wanted to. This is how I see it happening as an origin lore for the story following this: In the 100s BCE, the Marian reforms happen. However, Optimates senators ensure that land reform is decided by the Senate. Eventually, when the Mithridatic War happens, Marius fails to outmanuever Sulla, and Sulla goes to fight King Mithridates VI. Resentful, Marius uses his populist rhetoric, connections with Roman tribunes, and a sunken grain ship to incite a riot in Rome. This riot, later called the "Dimidiatio Senatus," resulted in the Roman Senate being attacked and half of the senators killed, with the majority of the remainder (all Populares senators) joining the rioters, and the surviving Optimates senators fleeing Rome to the countryside. Following the Dimidiatio Senatus, Marius declares the creation of the "Tribuni Romanae Res Publicae" (TRRP), or "Roman Tribunal Republic," denouncing the old Senate as a now-dead continuation of the old hated kingdom and their sycophants. Marius establishes a Tribunal Senate of people aligned with him (later called Marians) to govern Rome, then marches to Anatolia to fight Sulla. In a battle in Greece, Sulla defeats Marius and executes him. Sulla marches his legion into Italia. At Rome, Sulla finds a large citizen militia and the Roman city garrison opposing him, and a bloody battle begins. With the help of a certain Gaius Julius Caesar, Rome defeats Sulla, albeit it's a pyrrhic victory due to larger casualties on Rome's side. Sulla is beaten to death by a furious mob. Following the Battle of Rome, Caesar asks the Marian Tribunal Senate to entrust him with command of the Roman Army in the fight against remaining Patrician armies outside of Rome that seek to crush what Marius created. The Tribunal Senate trusts Caesar, and orders him to quash the opposition (later called Sullarians). In what is later known as the Sullarian War, Caesar crushes Patrician armies and confiscates the families' wealth and grants it to a Tribunal Senatorial Treasury, which is used as the central place of wealth of Rome, and funds from it are used to pay standard wages to soldiers. Caesar is a revered war hero, praised as Marius' heir. Caesar then relieves himself of command of the Sullarian Campaign, and suggests expanding Rome into Gaul. However, before his request his accepted, he suffers a stroke and dies. In the aftermath of the Sullarian War, around the 1st Century AD, the Tribunal Senate tries to stabilize the Tribunal Republic. The previous classifications of plebeian or patrician are abolished; Romans are just "Civii," or "Citizens" (Civis for singular). Additionally, some laws are established or confirmed, such as the ban on mobilized troops within Italia, the prohibition of army officials in public offices, and a system where Roman Provinces each elect two senators to the Tribunal Senate, plus two senators elected by the city of Rome itself to the Tribunal Senate. Following the Sullarian War, there is a huge cultural shift away from militarized politics and aristocracy. Two new factions emerge: the Marians, who are reformists loyal to Marius' rhetoric and believe in helping the common people and pragmatically responding to crises, and the Caesarians, radicals who idolize Caesar that believe that all aristocracy should be destroyed and the republic only serve the common people. In the decades that followed, Rome would gradually expand, but mainly by courting Celtic and Germanic tribes and negotiating integration into the Roman Tribunal Republic. New provinces emerge, and Celtic/Germanic warriors are used as mercenaries alongside Roman armies. Trade and commerce began to prosper, and so the Roman Navy was prioritized for funding and seen as less corruptible. Also, Christianity happens. However, it does not expand as fast because of a lack of a Constantine figure, and eventually becomes a recognized, non-persecuted religion within Rome, like the Roman Pantheon, Celtic paganism, Germanic paganism, and the slowly-dying Cult of Mithras. Basically, Rome slowly turns into a mercantile, seafaring republic with integration treaties with as many Celtic and Germanic tribes they could negotiate with. Kind of like a republican Carthage, ironically. Additionally, as wars reduce in scale and more non-Romans join provincial and senatorial administration, slavery is gradually banned. Persia remains a strategic rival over competition for Arabia and Mesopotamia, yet wars reduce in intensity and the rivalry turns mostly commercial. Rome expands through trade and treaties, sticking to the coast, where ships can easily transport goods and protect cities (again, Carthage-like and kinda Venice-like). It also trades with Aksum, Nubian Kingdoms south of Sudan, and sub-Saharan nations like Mali and Ghana (since North African coastal settlements reach Morocco and the Canary Islands eventually). Eventually, the Hunnic Invasions happen. Rome managed to better deal with the invasion thanks to greater stability, Germanic cooperation/mercenary armies, and more stable politics. The Tribunal Senate appoints a general to the position of "Caesar," which becomes the title of a military commander charged with winning a campaign vital to Rome's survival. The Huns are repelled, but Rome's maritime and mercantile economy is disrupted. In the aftermath, a young merchant named Cassius Atticus Felix emerges. A shrewd merchant and tactical investor, he focuses on creating merchant fleets and creating more merchant outposts along the Mediterranean and Mare Hibericum (the Atlantic Ocean). It is because of him that coastal cities in Morocco expanded as far west as they did, and he advocated for reduced taxes and regulations on Roman merchants, calling for "Mercator Autonomia," or "Merchant Autonomy," to revitalize Rome's economy and create prosperity. Cassius was heading to personally found a trading town on the Canary Islands when a hurricane hit the area and killed him. However, Cassius becomes immortalized as a rebuilder of post-Hun Rome's economy. The merchant class, and those sympathetic to them, form a new faction based on his ideals, called the Cassians. A while after this, conservative Romans who disliked the existence of "uncivilized barbarians" in Rome and merchant "luxury and decadence" form a traditionalist faction named the Catonians, named after Cato the Elder. They believe in the superiority of Roman culture, worship the old Roman/Greek Pantheon, oppose luxury, and don't oppose the idea of re-establishing slavery. Gradually, merchant oligarchy seeps into the Roman Tribunal Republic as merchants start buying out senators and provincial representatives. The Caesarians firmly oppose it, and so grow closer with the Catonians. Inside the Caesarian faction, a schism slowly begins to brew as those who oppose Catonian traditionalism and Romano-centrism clash with those who do support it. After some more tribal integration, province establishment, commerce expansion, and minor warfare, Mohammad creates Islam, and unites the Arab tribes (slowly being integrated by the Romans and the Persians) in opposition to them. Rome and Persia temporarily create a defensive pact against the Islamic Invasions, otherwise known as the "Crisis of the 7th Century." While Rome and Persia lost some cities along the coast of the Indian Ocean and the Persian Gulf, the Sasanian Empire retains Mesopotamia, and Rome defends the cities on the western coast of the Arabian peninsula, bordering the Red Sea and Judea. The Arabian Empire is then created as a religiously fanatical, militarized, yet mercantile and diplomatic empire. Islam still spreads through Islamic traders, though not as strongly in North Africa or the Mediterranean as a whole thanks to the Roman Tribunal Republic's stability and already existing religions. [By the first millennium CE, Rome's political system works like this:] [Provinces are ruled by Provincial Tribunes, elected by the people of the province from those who have not been in the military for at least four years. Additionally, some large cities, particularly coastal entrepot cities, become provinces in their own right. Each province can pass their own laws and manage their own administration, paying taxes to the Tribunal Treasury in Rome and following senatorial law]. [Each province (plus the city of Rome) elects two senators to represent them in the Tribunal Senate. No senator may have been in the military within the previous four years. The Tribunal Senate has no Consuls, instead having an "Orator," which is basically their Speaker. The longest-serving senator automatically becomes Orator. If the Senate passes a law, it can be vetoed by Provincial Tribunes if at least half of them vote on to veto the Senate law within one year of its passing. Provincial Tribunes may vote to send a law to the Senate for consideration, and if it is sent to the Senate and the Senate approves it, it cannot be vetoed no matter how many tribunes veto it]. [Caesars are appointed by the Senate in a time of dire war with a term of two years, after which point (if the war is still ongoing) the Senate can either replace them or affirm their trust in them. This repeats until the dire war is over]. In 1000 CE, to celebrate one thousand years of popular rule following the Dimidiatio Senatus, celebrations are held across Rome, and the Roman Tribunal Republic changes its formal name to the "Res Publica Inter Marium" (RPIM), or "Republic between seas," for the grand republic lies between multiple seas: Mare Ponticum (the Black Sea), Mare Mediterraneus (the Mediterranean Sea), Mare Hibericum (Atlantic Ocean west of Iberia and the Canary Islands), Mare Britannicum (the North Sea and Atlantic Ocean around Britain and Ireland), and Mare Rubrum (the Red Sea and Indian Ocean). Thoughts?

items.question: What If al-Andalus survives
human_answers: There are a number of good surviving Al Andalus timelines like moonlight in a jar on here. Obviously it can go however the author wants it- my suspicion though is that an Al Andalus which remains relatively centralised is more vulnerable than the taifas were otl to crusades- if the events over the next century don’t butterfly the Turkic incursions into Anatolia and the papal call to crusade, a crusade would certainly be directed towards Spain as well. A centralised state is often easier to conquer than decentralised ones, all you need is one battle that allows the conquerors access to the capital and central bureaucracy and you’ve done it. I think it’d be interesting to see such a fundamentally different pattern of reconquista, where instead of small northern principalities gradually extending southwards, one decisive battle/sack of Cordoba puts crusaders in charge of cordoba like happened in 1204 Constantinople, you end up with a Christian kingdom with Cordoba as its capital and likely a French king. This kingdom of Cordoba could be instantly much more powerful than the northern Christian kingdoms. Its administrative languages would be Latin and Arabic, and the language of the nobility (unlike otl) wouldn’t be an Iberian Romance language, more likely a northern French dialect, ruling over a population of Arabic and Mozarabic speakers. Unlike otl there would be no real reason for northern romance dialects to spread southwards, as even though northern Christians would settle the south, without state backing they’re more likely to assimilate to local Mozarabic or Arabic speaking Christian populations.

It wasn't unexpected, so to speak; he was ill throughout the year 1008, contracting the disease in February and dying in October. He had an angina attack. Whether this was caused by the illness, the stress of managing the country, or poisoning is difficult to say. Adding to that, instead of recovering in Cordoba, he spent a good part of the year campaigning, which probably didn't help. The reason Al-Muzaffar couldn't remain idle was the large number of problems he faced during his six-year reign. Early in his reign, there was a sharp decline in gold and silver coinage, which may indicate economic difficulties in al-Andalus or problems with the supply of gold and silver from Africa. A few months after succeeding his father, al-Muzaffar faced a conspiracy to assassinate him and his vizier, Ibn al-Qatta. The conspirators, with the commander of Saqaliba and the court secretary as the most prominent figures, intended to replace the hajib with his underage son, Muhammad, who would be a puppet (So, Puppet Squared), just as Caliph Hisham II had been. Al-Muzaffar, unlike his father, was a king-soldier, not a philosopher king (who had legal and literary training). Muzaffar had no interest in administration, politics, arts, or sciences. Leaving this to his vizier. Later, his vizier and friend, Ibn al-Qatta, who was married to his sister, organized a failed coup against Muzaffar. Al-Muzaffar, in a simple way, could not catch a break; it was one coup attempt followed by another assassination attempt, followed by another coup attempt. He had to kill people who were important to the functioning of the government during his father's era. During one of his campaigns in 1006, he attacked the territory of King Sancho Garces III of Pamplona and ended up being defeated in this campaign, which, along with his poor governance (partly due to numerous coups and open intrigue at court), brought him a bad reputation. To be honest, it was difficult to match his father's greatness. The government would remain in crisis because al-Muzaffar's biggest problem was that he was not a Umayyad, and anyone with ambition could find legitimacy in trying to dethrone him to establish the Umayyads (on paper). This, coupled with the fact that he was not as competent as his father (who was far superior), generated this crisis. Perhaps that's quite debatable. It could have been much worse or better; it depends on many factors. I don't know if he would last the rest of the century. Seriously, the kingdom is having serious internal problems. I don't know if it would last until 1020. The kingdom would collapse; the kingdom died informally when al-Mansur exterminated the Arab elite who had maintained the emirate/caliphate for the past centuries, replacing them with enslaved soldiers and Berbers. Al-Mansur possessed exceptional skill in managing the political, military, and ethnic intrigue of the kingdom. However, his son inherited the problems without possessing the necessary competence. He had to contend with enslaved soldiers and Berbers vying to become the new Al-Mansur, the remaining Arab elite wanting to return to power, pressure from the north, and governmental instability.

items.original_question: What if al-Andalus survives The 11th century was a pivotal moment in Hispanic history. At the beginning of the century, the Caliphate of Córdoba was the dominant power on the peninsula. The city of Córdoba rivaled Constantinople as the largest city in Europe. Ostensibly ruled by the Umayyads under Caliph Hisham II, in reality he was merely a puppet of his ambitious hajib (chamberlain) Abu Amir Muhammad ‘ al-Mansur ’ more famously known as Almanzor. A highly ambitious man, Almanzor would import thousands of Berber tribesmen into al-Andalus to serve in Córdoba’s army. He would utilize this army to not only keep the disgruntled Arab elites in line but also to bring the Christian north to heel through large-scale annual raids. While this arrangement put strain on the treasury and created ethnic strife, it was effective, and upon his death in 1002 AD Almanzor would be seamlessly succeeded by his son al-Muzaffar. Al-Muzaffar would continue his father’s regime, continuing to import Berbers, continuing to raid the north, and keeping the state stable. It was looking like a dual-power dynamic was emerging in Córdoba just as it had back east in Baghdad. However, while on campaign against Castile, al-Muzaffar would die unexpectedly in 1008 AD. His younger brother Sanchuelo would succeed him as hajib , but he would lack the brilliance of his father or the prudence of his brother. Sanchuelo would offend the Arab nobility by having Hisham II name him as his heir as Caliph. This act would trigger the Fitna of al-Andalus, reducing the grand city of Córdoba to ruins and shattering the country into 30+ squabbling petty kingdoms or taifas. Suddenly, the power dynamic was reversed. Now the Muslim south was paying tribute to the Christian north. The north would consolidate under the Jiménez dynasty, and then push south, culminating in the capture of Toledo in 1085 AD, followed by the occupation of the rest of al-Andalus by the Berber Almoravid dynasty from Morocco. The rest of the Reconquista would unfold in the following centuries. The Fitna proved to be a lucky break for Christian Iberia, as without the might of Córdoba crushing them, the Reconquista started to truly gain steam. However, what if the Fitna was averted or delayed by having al-Muzaffar not die prematurely in 1008? Had he not died young, Sanchuelo likely never comes to power. This alone averts the triggering of the Fitna . Of course, the underlying financial issues and ethnic strife still exist, so the Fitna may still occur under different circumstances. However it’s likely to be nowhere as devestating for al-Andalus as IOTL. How would a continuing Caliphate of Córdoba navigate the rest of the 11th century? Would al-Andalus remain powerful and prosperous as we transition into the High Middle Ages? Could the Andalusi withstand pressure from both Christians and Berbers alike? Will the Reconquista ever happen without al-Andalus collapsing?

I don’t know if he’d be able to gain the loyalty of his siblings seen as Frankish traditions would still be pushed for.
